body:
[SIPHONED VERDICT]: The US government simultaneously claims Iran's military is 'almost wiped out' and has suppressed the commercial satellite evidence that would allow anyone else to verify or falsify that claim. The very imagery the US government uses to assess Iranian capabilities has been restricted from public view by the US government itself — creating a verification black hole where the administration controls both the evidence and the characterization of it. WaPo's 109-image cross-referenced investigation, corroborated by named US officials on background and by CSIS analysis, puts the damage at 228 structures and $800 million across 15 bases. Iran has been publishing verified satellite imagery of the same strikes through state media with no comparable suppression constraint.

On July 10, 2026, the Washington Post published a satellite-imagery investigation corroborating Iranian state media's coverage of damage to US military infrastructure across the Middle East. The WaPo investigation — based on 109 independently verified Iranian satellite images, cross-referenced against European Union satellite imagery and the limited available Planet Labs data — found that Iranian strikes damaged or destroyed at least 228 structures and pieces of equipment across at least 15 US military sites in eight countries since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran in late February 2026. The estimated damage: approximately $800 million in destruction of US air defence systems, aircraft, radar, communications equipment, and fuel infrastructure.

The physical record runs directly against two concurrent US government narratives. The first is the White House's repeated claim that Iran's military has been "almost wiped out" by US strikes. The second is the Pentagon's public characterization of base damage as "limited." The WaPo finding — confirmed by named US officials speaking on background — is that some bases were rendered too dangerous to staff at normal levels and commanders moved most personnel out of range of Iranian fire at the start of the conflict.

The suppression mechanism that makes this story possible: since mid-March, two major commercial satellite providers, Vantor and Planet Labs, have been complying with a US government request to "limit, delay or indefinitely withhold" publication of imagery of the region. Iran International, a London-based satellite channel, and BBC Verify both note that Iranian state media has been publishing high-resolution satellite images throughout the war — images that, when verified against EU satellite data, have proven authentic and unmanipulated.

The named experts WaPo cites offer assessments that contradict official US government characterizations. Mark Cancian of CSIS: "The damage to US bases in the region has been underreported." Dr. Kelly Grieco of the Stimson Centre: the US military "appears to have been guilty of a degree of early-war complacency" in failing to adapt to Iran's tactical evolution from barrages to precision strikes. Vice-Admiral Mark Mellett: THAAD batteries are at the core of a "highly complex" regional defence network that "cannot be quickly or easily replaced" — directly contradicting the "almost wiped out" framing for Iranian military capability.

The $800 million damage figure — higher than previously reported — comes from CSIS analysis corroborated by the WaPo investigation. The 42 aircraft (F-15, F-35, MQ-9 Reaper, A-10), 24 drones, and multiple THAAD and Patriot battery components destroyed are catalogued and verifiable via satellite imagery that the US government has suppressed from the public record.

The symmetric suppression paradox is the structural finding: the US government — the world's largest consumer of commercial satellite imagery, making Vantor and Planet Labs its biggest customers — has restricted those same companies from publishing evidence of the damage sustained in the conflict. Iran, meanwhile, has published verified satellite imagery of the same strikes through state media with no comparable suppression constraint. The evidentiary asymmetry — US suppressing the verification layer while Iran publishes it freely — means the only publicly available satellite record of US base damage in this conflict comes from Iranian state media.
narrative: The article's load-bearing finding is the symmetric suppression paradox: the US government simultaneously claims Iran's military is degraded ('almost wiped out') and has suppressed the commercial satellite evidence that would allow anyone else to verify or falsify that claim. The very imagery the US government uses to assess Iranian capabilities has been restricted from public view by the US government itself — creating a verification black hole where the administration controls both the evidence and the characterization of it. Meanwhile, Iranian state media's verified satellite imagery of the same strikes is freely available. The asymmetry — Iran publishing verified satellite evidence, the US suppressing it — is the structural finding.
analysis: The 228 structures / $800M damage figure is verified by 109 cross-referenced images in WaPo's investigation, corroborated by named US officials on background and by CSIS analysis. The Vantor/Planet suppression mechanism is documented as a stated US government policy with named company compliance. The 'almost wiped out' narrative is physically contradicted by the damage catalog (42 aircraft, 24 drones, THAAD/Patriot battery components) that the suppressed imagery would show. The named expert assessments from Cancian, Grieco, and Mellett are all on-record characterizations that contradict official US government framing. The structural asymmetry — US suppressing the very evidence it uses to assess Iranian capabilities, while Iran publishes equivalent imagery freely — is documented and self-consistent.
